A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SAE-based diffusion-model interpretability work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: V3 reports original SAE reconstruction experiments, RIEBench comparisons, feature analyses, and qualitative interventions on SDXL and FLUX, including appendix results.

after.justification: V5 retains original empirical results and adds quantitative block ablations, a classifier-free-guidance comparison, and FLUX RIEBench evaluations.

M1.justification: The SAE architecture, training objectives, and selected training blocks remain unchanged. RIEBench interventions change: v3 preserves source spatial information for several edit types, whereas v5 uses uniform masked updates throughout. Deletion also changes from contrasting the target object with its background to comparing source and target activations within the target mask.

E1.justification: Both versions use LAION-COCO, LAION-5B, the same nine PIEBench-derived editing categories, and texture evaluation data. SDXL Turbo, SDXL Base, and FLUX already appear in v3. The added FLUX RIEBench evaluation and replaced illustrative prompts remain within existing data and task coverage.

E2.justification: Neuron and activation-steering baselines remain the principal RIEBench comparators, but their transport implementations are revised alongside SAE transport to use spatially averaged, uniform masked updates. The neuron, PCA, random, and other controls in the feature-specificity comparison remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Figure 5 changes from absolute CLIP similarity to CLIP increase. Neuron transport budgets change from 5,000-80,000 to 12,800-204,800, and SAE/neuron strengths change from 1 and 2 to 0.5, 1, and 1.5. V5 also adds FLUX single-versus-multiple-layer evaluation protocols and quantitative block ablations averaged over 20 prompts.

E4.justification: V5 adds a conditional/unconditional intervention ablation for classifier-free guidance (Figure 7), extends qualitative attention-block ablation with quantitative attention and ResNet ablations (Table 1), and compares single-layer with multiple-layer FLUX interventions (Appendix F). These investigate guidance behavior, omitted block types, and intervention placement beyond v3's analyses.

E5.justification: V3 Appendix H.2 and v5 Appendix I.2 retain the same mean/standard-deviation reporting, baseline sampling description, and confidence-interval approximation. Figure 3's uncertainty shading is retained. The new 20-prompt ablation specifies an evaluation sample size, without introducing a new repeated-run or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Under revised settings, Figure 5 replaces v3's reported SAE advantage in all categories except deletion with broadly similar performance, a neuron advantage at higher LPIPS for changing objects, and poor pose editing. V5 adds FLUX results and quantitative block scores, including LPIPS 0.851 for ablating up_blocks.2.resnets.2. These are revised or additional results, not same-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: The SAE objectives, superposition reasoning, and Johnson-Lindenstrauss bound are retained. Expanded timestep/layer notation and the explicit neuron-ranking equation spell out aggregation and normalized absolute-difference ranking already described in v3. No new theorem, proof, or substantive theoretical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The RIEBench contribution shifts from finer-grained editing than neuron and steering baselines to matching neuron performance with orders of magnitude fewer features. Section 6 also newly conjectures applicability to most of thousands of SDXL and FLUX adaptations. These materially revise comparative and generalization claims, although the abstract's central one-step SAE claim remains unchanged.

C2.justification: V5 adds explanations of guidance-related cancellation, possible normalization effects behind multiple-layer FLUX interventions, and difficulties with pose and deletion edits. Section 6 introduces explicit limitations concerning cross-block features, global/compositional control, and hyperparameter dependence, alongside a new interpretation connecting transfer across model adaptations to model merging.

D1.justification: V5 newly documents classifier-free-guidance handling, expands neuron-selection details, and specifies the FLUX intervention span through layer 56. It adds an explicit SDLens repository link and SDXL Base/FLUX application links. The existing SAE training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V5 adds Model Soups by Wortsman et al. and Learning on Model Weights Using Tree Experts by Horwitz et al. to motivate transfer between related fine-tuned models. The existing related-work discussion and other cited works are substantially retained.

P1.justification: Generalization and RIEBench explanations are expanded and locally rewritten, and the appendix's nine intervention recipes are consolidated into three groups. A dedicated SDXL Base appendix and limitations paragraph are added. The overall section sequence and much of the prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 5 is redesigned from densely labelled scatterplots into curves with consistent scales and structured legends. Figure 4 is redrawn, RIEBench example grids are recomposed, and new guidance/FLUX figures and a block-ablation table are added. Many existing appendix illustrations and tables are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: V5's wider RIEBench sweeps support a more qualified sparsity advantage, while new guidance, block-ablation, and quantitative FLUX analyses improve evaluation and practical explanation beyond v3's largely illustrative FLUX evidence. The net gain is limited by the untested extrapolation to thousands of model adaptations and Figure 14's omission of configurations that fail to improve CLIP similarity.
